card.stem: The main door of a house is an insulated wooden door with 12 mm cedar sheeting on both sides, as shown. The door is fitted in a 400 mm concrete block external wall with a full-fill insulated cavity. The wall is rendered on both sides. The doorframe is 150 mm × 70 mm and the door is 90 mm in thickness.
card.questionText: To a scale of 1:5 draw a vertical section through the top of the door, showing the wall, the concrete lintels over the door, the doorframe and the door. Show the typical construction details from 400 mm below the lintels to a level 400 mm above the lintels. Include three typical dimensions on your drawing.

rows.contextNote: Any 7 of the above details ( 5 marks each). Credit the best SEVEN acceptable details at 5 marks each, capped at 35. Marked details: 19 mm external render; 100 mm block outer leaf; 200 mm full-fill cavity insulation; DPC; 100 mm block inner leaf; 15 mm plaster with skim; reinforced concrete lintels; 18 mm plywood with airtightness seal; insulated plasterboard with skim; proprietary cavity closer; 150 × 70 mm doorframe; 90 mm door top rail and insulation; 12 mm vertical sheeting both sides.

options: 18 mm plywood with airtightness seal to wall and doorframe
90 mm door top rail and insulation
12 mm vertical sheeting to both sides of the door

rows.contextNote: Three appropriate typical dimensions on the section, 1 each.

card.stem: The external wall of a new house has a 100 mm concrete block outer leaf, a cavity and a 200 mm inner leaf of timber frame construction, as shown. The inner leaf is insulated and insulated plasterboard is also fixed to the timber studs.
card.questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches show how the inner leaf is to be insulated. Specify the type and thickness of insulation.

rows.verbatim: How the inner leaf is insulated - Sketches
rows.contextNote: Sketches showing the inner leaf (5) and its insulation (5), as in the scheme’s model sketch.

rows.verbatim: How the inner leaf is insulated - Notes
rows.contextNote: Two valid details, 4 each. Such as: insulation placed between the uprights; structural sheeting board fixed to the uprights for rigidity; a breather membrane; the airtightness/vapour barrier on the warm side; insulated plasterboard fitted inside.
Such as: blown cellulose, sheep’s wool, fibreglass, woodfibre, cork, mineral fibre batts or spray foam, at least 200 mm thick.

card.questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: handrail; box dovetail joint; purlin; damp-proof course; ball valve; energy rating; wind turbine; joist hanger; service cavity.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Hand rail: the solid member fitted to the newel posts, parallel to the pitch line, carried on the balusters; generally 75 × 50 mm, jointed to the newel by mortise and tenon, 900–1000 mm above the pitch line. Box dovetail joint: a joint of tails and pins for box shapes and drawers in high-quality furniture, by hand or with jigs; dovetail slope 1:6 in softwood and 1:8 in hardwood; decorative with contrasting woods. Purlin: the member under the rafters giving them support and alignment in a traditional cut roof, typically 175 × 75 mm, carried on struts to an internal load-bearing wall or on a steel joist. Damp-proof course: an impermeable barrier, usually heavy plastic, in external and internal walls, linked to the damp-proof membrane, 150 mm above ground; stops rising damp and damp crossing the cavity at openings. Ball valve: controls the water entering a cistern or tank: a float rises with the water and closes the valve; mounted on the side of the cistern and connected to the supply. Energy rating: labels rating appliances, and homes through the Building Energy Rating, from A (most efficient, lowest bills) to G, to help consumers choose. Wind turbine: converts wind energy to mechanical energy and then electricity through its blades, generator and tower; small or large scale, sited for the wind; an eco-friendly source of energy. Joist hanger: a galvanised steel hanger wrapping three sides of a joist end, nailed or screwed through predrilled holes, anchoring floor, ceiling and decking joists; stronger than nails alone. Service cavity: a separate cavity on the inside of an external wall carrying wiring and plumbing so they do not damage the airtightness membrane; used in solid and timber frame walls.
